anchors.text: Fig. 1 This figure shows how the critical shoulder angle (CSA) was determined. The critical shoulder angle was defined as the angle between a line connecting the inferior glenoid border to the lateral acromion border and a line running from the inferior to the superior glenoid border.

Fig. 2 The figure shows the measurement of acromial slope (AS). To measure acromial slope, the midpoint of the inferior acromion was established. A line was drawn between the most anterior edge of the acromion and the midpoint. A second line was drawn between the most posterior rim of the acromion and the midpoint of the inferior acromion. Acromial slope was defined as the angle between these two lines.

Fig. 3 The figure shows how acromial tilt (AT) was determined. Acromial tilt was defined as the angle between a line connecting the anterior and posterior margins of the acromion and a line extending from the posterior margin of the acromion to the distal end of the coracoid.

Fig. 4 The figure shows how the lateral acromial angle (LAA) was determined. First, a line was drawn between the superior and inferior rims of the glenoid. A second line, parallel and tangential to the inferior surface of the acromion, was then traced. The lateral acromial angle was defined as the angle between the two lines.

Fig. 5 The figure shows how the acromial index was determined. A line was drawn to connect the superior and inferior borders of the glenoid and defined as the glenoid plane. A second line, parallel to the glenoid plane, was drawn at the most lateral point of the acromion and defined as the acromion plane. Finally, a third line was drawn at the most lateral point of the humeral head and defined as the humeral head plane. The acromial index was calculated by dividing the distance between the glenoid and acromion planes (A) from that between the glenoid and humeral planes (B).

Fig. 6 The figure represents the receiver operating characteristic curve of the acromiohumeral interval and acromial slope. The coordinates on the curve determined the cutoff values for identifying a retear: 7.4 mm for the acromiohumeral interval and 24.5° for acromial slope. A color image accompanies the online version of this article.

anchors.text: Fig. 1. Mechanisms of PEMF leading to angiogenesis. PEMF activates VGCC and calcium influx induces intracellular calcium accumulation. PEMF promotes the binding of calcium to calmodulin. Calcium/calmodulin then activates NOS, catalyst NO release. NO raises cGMP levels, which promotes growth factor release, inducing paracrine and autocrine effects. anchors.text: Figure 1. Construction and performance evaluation of injectable Piezoelectric hydrogels. (A) Schematic diagram of the “sol–gel” transition effect in injectable Piezoelectric hydrogels. (B) Image depicting the shear-thinning behavior and injectability of the hydrogel. (C and D) Shear-thinning effect of injectable Piezoelectric hydrogel. (E–G) Self-healing ability of injectable Piezoelectric hydrogel.

Figure 2. Material characterization of the PVA/CNF/BTO@PDA (Piezoelectric) hydrogel. (A) FTIR spectroscopy of CNF, BTO, PDA, PVA, and PVA/CNF/BTO@PDA. (B and C) X-ray diffraction of CNF, BTO, and PVA/CNF/BTO@PDA. (D and E) DSC thermograms were obtained for the PVA hydrogel within a temperature range of -40 to 40 °C, while the PVA/CNF/BTO@PDA hydrogel was analyzed over a broader range of 0 to 130 °C. (F) Wettability comparison between the PVA/CNF hydrogel and PVA/CNF/BTO@PDA hydrogel. (G and H) Second harmonic generation (SHG) image of the BTO nanoflake along the PVA/CNF/BTO@PDA hydrogel. (I–K) Piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM) images (out-of-plane) of the PVA/CNF/BTO@PDA hydrogel. The data are presented as the means ± SD (n = 3). A two-sided paired Student’s t test was used to calculate statistical differences. **P < 0.01.

Figure 3. Electrical stimulation produced by the Piezoelectric hydrogel enhanced the osteogenic/tenogenic differentiation of BMSCs. (A and B) ALP staining and Alizarin Red staining at 7 and 14 days of osteogenic induction of BMSCs with electrical stimulation produced by the Piezoelectric hydrogel; scale bar, 100  $ \mu $m. (C and D) Analysis of ALP staining and Alizarin Red staining data showed that the positive rate of calcium nodules in the Piezo-3  $ \mu $A group was significantly higher than that in other groups. The data are presented as the means  $ \pm $ SD (n = 3). A two-sided paired Student’s t test was used to calculate statistical differences.  $ ^{\#}P > 0.05 $,  $ ^{*}P < 0.05 $. (E and F) Immunofluorescence staining of biomarkers of BMSC osteogenesis (RUNX-2 and OPN) at 7 days with electrical stimulation produced by the Piezoelectric hydrogel; scale bar, 20  $ \mu $m. (G and H) Fluorescence value analysis of RUNX-2 and OPN immunofluorescent staining showed that the Piezo-3  $ \mu $A group was significantly higher than that in other groups. (I and J) Fluorescence value analysis of TNMD and Scx immunofluorescent staining showed that the Piezo-5  $ \mu $A group was significantly higher than that in other groups. The data are presented as the means  $ \pm $ SD (n = 3). (One-way ANOVA.)  $ ^{\#}P > 0.05 $,  $ ^{*}P < 0.05 $. (K and L) Immunofluorescence staining of biomarkers of BMSC tenogenic differentiation (TNMD and Scx) at 7 days with electrical stimulation produced by the Piezoelectric hydrogel; scale bar, 20  $ \mu $m (UP, unpolarized; Piezo, Piezoelectric hydrogel).

Figure 4. Electrical stimulation produced by the Piezoelectric hydrogel regulated the macrophage polarization of RAW 264.7. (A and B) Immunofluorescence staining of CD68 (biomarker of M0 macrophage), iNOS (biomarker of M1 macrophage), and CD206 (biomarker of M2 macrophage) at 7 and 14 days of RAW 264.7 macrophage with electrical stimulation produced by the Piezoelectric hydrogel. (C and D) Cytoskeleton staining at 7 and 14 days of RAW 264.7 macrophage; scale bar, 20  $ \mu $m. (E and F) Fluorescence value analysis of CD206 at 7 days showed that the Piezo-3  $ \mu $A group was significantly higher than that in other groups. (G) The filament length of RAW 264.7 macrophage pseudopod at 7 days showed that the Piezo-3  $ \mu $A group was significantly longer than the other groups. (H and I) Fluorescence value analysis of CD206 at 14 days showed that the Piezo-3  $ \mu $A group was significantly higher than that in other groups. (J) The filament length of RAW 264.7 macrophage pseudopod at 14 days showed that the Piezo-3  $ \mu $A group was significantly longer than that in other groups. The data are presented as the means  $ \pm $ SD (n = 3). (One-way ANOVA). #P > 0.05, *P < 0.05 (UP, unpolarized; Piezo, Piezoelectric hydrogel).

Figure 5. Electrical stimulation produced by the Piezoelectric hydrogel regulated the macrophage polarization of RAW 264.7 in the  $ H_2O_2 $ and IL- $ 1\beta $ inflammation environment. (A and B) Immunofluorescence staining of CD68 (biomarker of M0 macrophage), iNOS (biomarker of M1 macrophage), and CD206 (biomarker of M2 macrophage) at 7 days of RAW 264.7 macrophage with electrical stimulation produced by the Piezoelectric hydrogel in  $ H_2O_2 $ and IL- $ 1\beta $ inflammation environment. (C and D) Immunofluorescence staining of CD68, iNOS, and CD206 at 14 days of RAW 264.7 macrophage; scale bar, 20  $ \mu $m. (E) Fluorescence value analysis of CD206 at 7 and 14 days showed that the Piezo-3  $ \mu $A and Piezo-5  $ \mu $A groups were significantly higher than that in other groups. (F) Fluorescence value analysis of iNOS at 7 and 14 days showed that the Piezo-3  $ \mu $A and Piezo-5  $ \mu $A groups were significantly lower than  $ H_2O_2 $ and IL- $ 1\beta $ groups, as well as the Nonpiezo and UP+Piezo groups. The data are presented as the means  $ \pm $ SD (n = 3). (One-way ANOVA.)  $ ^{\#}P > 0.05 $,  $ ^{**}P < 0.01 $.

Figure 6. Electrical stimulation produced by the Piezoelectric hydrogel regulated BMSC osteogenic/tenogenic differentiation in  $ H_{2}O_{2} $ and IL-1 $ \beta $ inflammation environments. (A and B) Immunofluorescence staining of biomarkers of BMSC osteogenesis (OPN) at 7 days with electrical stimulation produced by the Piezoelectric hydrogel in a  $ H_{2}O_{2} $ and IL-1 $ \beta $ inflammation environment. (C and D) Immunofluorescence staining of biomarkers of BMSC tenogenic differentiation (Scx) at 7 days with electrical stimulation produced by the Piezoelectric hydrogel in a  $ H_{2}O_{2} $ and IL-1 $ \beta $ inflammation environment; scale bar, 20  $ \mu $m. (E) Fluorescence value analysis of OPN at 7 days showed that the Piezo-3  $ \mu $A group was significantly higher than that in other groups. (F) Fluorescence value analysis of Scx at 7 days showed that the Piezo-5  $ \mu $A group was significantly higher than that in other groups. The data are presented as the means  $ \pm $ SD (n = 3) (One-way ANOVA)  $ \#P > 0.05 $,  $ *P < 0.01 $ (UP, unpolarized; Piezo, Piezoelectric hydrogel).

Figure 7. Electrical stimulation produced by the Piezoelectric hydrogel reduced the ROS and improved mitochondrial function in  $ H_{2}O_{2} $ and IL-1 $ \beta $ inflammation environment at 7 days. (A and B) Immunofluorescence staining of the content of intracellular ROS at 7 days with electrical stimulation produced by the Piezoelectric hydrogel in a  $ H_{2}O_{2} $ and IL-1 $ \beta $ inflammation environment. (C and D) Immunofluorescence staining of the JC-1 probe at 7 days with electrical stimulation produced by the Piezoelectric hydrogel in  $ H_{2}O_{2} $ and IL-1 $ \beta $ inflammation environment; scale bar, 20  $ \mu $m. (E) Fluorescence value analysis of the content of intracellular ROS showed that the Piezo-3  $ \mu $A and Piezo-5  $ \mu $A groups were significantly lower than in other groups. (F) The JC-1 ratios of mitochondrial function indicate that the Piezo-3  $ \mu $A and Piezo-5  $ \mu $A groups were significantly higher than that in  $ H_{2}O_{2} $ and IL-1 $ \beta $ groups, as well as the Nonpiezo and UP+Piezo groups. The data are presented as the means  $ \pm $ SD (n = 3). (One-way ANOVA).  $ \#P > 0.05 $,  $ ^{**}P < 0.01 $. (G) TEM of mitochondria structure in  $ H_{2}O_{2} $ and IL-1 $ \beta $ inflammation environment showed that the mitochondria in the  $ H_{2}O_{2} $ and IL-1 $ \beta $ groups were swollen and deformed with a relatively small number, while in the Piezo-3  $ \mu $A and Piezo-5  $ \mu $A groups, the morphology of mitochondria was relatively normal; scale bar, 2  $ \mu $m (UP, unpolarized; Piezo, Piezoelectric hydrogel).

Figure 8. Piezoelectric hydrogel promoted invasion and recruitment of BMSCs in vitro and in vivo. (A) Schematic diagram of the BMSCs/Macrophage/Piezoelectric hydrogel coculture system by the Flexcell Tissue Train system. (B and C) Coculture with Macrophage/Piezoelectric hydrogel promoted invasion of BMSCs in the Transwell assay and scratch assay at 7 and 14 days; scale bar, 100  $ \mu $m. (D and E) Statistical analysis of crystal violet cell number in Transwell assay and healing distance measurement in scratch assay. The data are presented as the means  $ \pm $ SD (n = 3). Two-sided paired Student's t test was used to calculate statistical differences.  $ ^{\#}P > 0.05 $,  $ ^{**}P < 0.01 $. (F) In vivo bioluminescence images to study exogenous DIO-labeled BMSCs recruited to the rotator cuff injury site. (G) Fluorescence value analysis of DIO-labeled BMSCs showed that the Piezo group was higher than other groups on 1 day and 1, 2, 4, and 8 weeks. The data are presented as the means  $ \pm $ SD (n = 3). (One-way ANOVA.) (H) Analysis of the M2/M1 ratio of macrophage in the rotator cuff injury site indicated that the Piezo group was higher than other groups on 1 day and 1, 2, 4, and 8 weeks. The data are presented as the means  $ \pm $ SD (n = 3). (One-way ANOVA.)  $ ^{\#}P > 0.05 $,  $ ^{**}P < 0.01 $. (I) Immunofluorescence staining of CD68 (biomarker of M0 macrophage), iNOS (biomarker of M1 macrophage), and CD206 (biomarker of M2 macrophage) on 1 day and 1, 2, 4, and 8 weeks of macrophages in the rotator cuff injury site; scale bar, 20  $ \mu $m (Piezo, Piezoelectric hydrogel).

Figure 9. Degradation of Piezoelectric hydrogel and macrophage polarization in vitro and in vivo. (A) The gross view of Piezoelectric hydrogel in PBS solution and medium solution in vitro. (B) The gross view of Piezoelectric hydrogel on subcutaneous rat model and H&E staining; scale bar, 2 mm. (C and D) The degradation kinetics of Piezoelectric hydrogel were evaluated in both PBS solution and medium over time intervals of 1, 2, 4, and 8 weeks, which demonstrated that the hydrogel exhibited progressive degradation across all time points; scale bar, 10  $ \mu $m. (E) The degradation kinetics of Piezoelectric hydrogel were evaluated on a subcutaneous rat model. The data are presented as the means  $ \pm $ SD (n=3). (One-way ANOVA). #P > 0.05, *P < 0.05. (F) Immunohistochemical staining of macrophages within the hydrogel on subcutaneous rat model at 1, 2, 4, and 8 weeks; scale bar, 10  $ \mu $m. (G and H) Fluorescence value analysis of CD206 showed that 4 weeks was significantly higher than that in other groups, and iNOS decreased over time. The data are presented as the means  $ \pm $ SD (n=3). (One-way ANOVA.) #P > 0.05, *P < 0.05.

Figure 10. Micro-CT images and 7T MRI of repaired rotator cuff tendon in vivo. (A and B) Representative 3D micro-CT images (sagittal, coronal, and horizontal sections) of humerus bone connected with repaired rotator cuff tendon at 4 and 8 weeks after Piezoelectric hydrogel treatment. (C and D) 7T MRI images of repaired rotator cuff tendon at 4 and 8 weeks; scale bar, 1 mm. (E and F) Comparison of Tb.Th and BMD in newly formed bone at 4 weeks. (G and H) Comparison of Tb.Th and BMD in newly formed bone at 8 weeks. The data are presented as the means ± SD (n = 6 shoulders). (One-way ANOVA.)  $ ^{*}P < 0.05 $ (Piezo, Piezoelectric hydrogel).

Figure 11. The histological evaluation and type II/I collagen expression of repaired rotator cuff tendon in vivo at 4 weeks. (A and B) H&E staining and Safranin O staining of repaired rotator cuff showed fibrous tissues with increased cellularity and vascularity appeared at the BTI in all repair groups after 4 postoperative weeks. (C and D) Masson's trichrome staining and Sirius Red staining of neo-rotator cuff tissue showed that the Piezo group's neo-rotator cuff tissue was rich in type I collagen fibers in the neo-rotator cuff tissue, while the fibrocartilage layer at the tendon-bone interface was rich in type II collagen fibers. (E and F) Type II collagen and type I collagen immunohistochemical staining of repaired rotator cuff tendon containing regenerated enthesis at 4 weeks. The boxes in the lower image of each staining are exhibited at a higher magnification of BTI. B, bone; T, tendon; I, interface; scale bar, 1 mm. (G and H) Analysis of tendon maturing score and metachromasia area in repaired rotator cuff tendon showed that the tendon maturation score in the Piezo group was significantly higher than that in the Suture and Nonpiezo groups. (I and J) Expression of type II collagen and type I collagen through immunohistochemical staining showed that the type II/I collagen in the Piezo group was higher than in other groups. The data are presented as the means ± SD (n = 6 shoulders). (One-way ANOVA.) *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001 (Piezo, Piezoelectric hydrogel).

anchors.text: Figure 1: Hill-Sachs Lesion (a) Grashey view of the shoulder shows malalignment of the glenohumeral joint; (b) Anteroposterior view shows the classic terminal position of the humeral head in a subcoracoid-type of anterior dislocation; (c) Impaction of the posterolateral surface of humeral head against anterior glenoid rim produces the Line of Condensation known as the Hill-Sachs lesion (arrow).

Figure 2: Broken Circle Method (a) This technique applies to internal rotation radiographs. A ROI circle is placed over the humeral head cortex. A line is drawn along axis of the bone, bisecting the humeral head corresponding to the 12 o'clock position. A perpendicular line corresponds to the 3- and the 9 o'clock positions. Adequate rotation is confirmed when the lateral margin of the intertubercular groove is medial to the long axis reference line (arrow); (b) When a Hill-Sachs impaction defect occurs in the 10 or 11 o'clock zones, it is a positive sign (1 or 2 o'clock in the opposite shoulder). [Used with permission from Yu JS, et al [7]].

Figure 3: Positive Broken Circle Sign (a) A reduced shoulder shows a Hill-Sachs lesion (arrow); (b) Note that after applying the Broken Circle method, the top of the defect breaks the circle at the 11 o'clock position; (c) Axial fluid-sensitive MR image shows the position and size of the impaction defect (arrow). [Used with permission from Yu JS, et al [7]].

Figure 4: Osseous Bankart Lesion (a) Grashey view an area of increased density in the inferior glenoid rim (arrow); (b) The magnified AP view shows a distracted curvilinear fracture fragment projecting anterior to the anteroinferior rim of the glenoid (arrow).

Figure 5: Greater Tuberosity Fracture (a) Grashey view shows a displaced fracture of the greater tuberosity in an anteriorly dislocated GH joint (arrow); (b) The anteroposterior view shows a Hill-Sachs lesion after reduction of the shoulder (arrow).

Figure 7: Reverse Osseous Bankart Lesion Axillary view (a) and axial CT image in the same patient show a small subtle fracture in the posterior rim (white arrows in a and b). Note the trough lesion from impaction of the anteromedial aspect of the humeral head (black arrows in a and b).

Figure 8: Lesser Tuberosity Fracture (a) Anteroposterior view shows a displaced fracture of the lesser tuberosity (arrow); (b) An axial CT images in the same patient show that the tuberosity fragment (white arrow) is slightly rotated at the leading edge of a trough lesion (black arrow).

Figure 8: Lesser Tuberosity Fracture (a) Anteroposterior view shows a displaced fracture of the lesser tuberosity (arrow); (b) An axial CT images in the same patient show that the tuberosity fragment (white arrow) is slightly rotated at the leading edge of a trough lesion (black arrow).

Figure 10: Broken Arch Sign (a) Grashey view shows disruption of the scapulohumeral arch (white lines). In a normal shoulder, these lines should connect to form a smooth arch; (b) Grashey view in another patient shows angulation of the scapulohumeral arch (white lines).

Figure 11: Absent Half-Moon Sign (a) Anteroposterior view shows loss of the normal overlap between the medial aspect of the humeral head and the glenoid fossa; (b) Anteroposterior view in a normal shoulder shows the typical expected overlap of the bones (oval).

Figure 6: Trough Lesion (a) Grashey view shows a vertically-oriented curvilinear density in the medial aspect of the humeral head (arrows) and malalignment of the glenohumeral joint; (b) Axillary view shows that the anterior aspect of the humeral head is impacted (arrow) and perched against the posterior rim of the glenoid.

Figure 1:
Normophysiology and pathophysiology of articular cartilage and bone in an osteochondral structure. (A) Healthy osteochondral tissue and (B) a magnified view of the interface. The tissue can be damaged either by (C) focal defects (cartilage partial thickness, cartilage full thickness, and bone) or degenerative conditions such as (D) osteoarthritis.

Figure 2:
Potential mechanical testing configurations. (A) Lap shear testing and (B) pull-apart testing can be used to assess the interface mechanics of biphasic materials. It should be noted that the use of gluing or clamping can be interchanged between the illustrated testing setups (i.e., clamping for lap shear and glue for pull apart). The axis in which the samples are pulled is denoted by blue arrows.

Figure 3:

Strategies for engineering an osteochondral implant. (A) Scaffold-based approaches have used primary cells or stem cells induced to differentiate toward a chondrogenic or osteogenic phenotype using bioactive factors. While culturing bone and cartilage cells separately upon seeding can aid in differentiation, engineering a robust interface between scaffolds is challenging. Alternatively, co-culture methods may be utilized to differentiate cells down chondrogenic and osteogenic lineages simultaneously. (B) Recently, self-assembled cartilage has been incorporated with a bone substrate to form osteochondral implants. If neocartilage is combined with a bone substrate at an early enough stage within tissue development, a robust interface is formed.

Figure 4:
(A) Arthroscopic image of chondral delamination failure of a condylar osteochondral allograft transplantation (OCA). (B) Sagittal MRI of chondral delamination failure of a transplanted patellar OCA (yellow arrow). (C) Clinically, it has been suggested that a larger discrepancy between the implant interface and native tissue interface (denoted by  $ {}^{TM} $) may lead to higher rates of delamination. Figures 4A and 4B were originally published by and used with permission from Dove Medical Press Ltd. Orthopedic Research and Reviews 2022:14 263-274.

anchors.text: Figure 1. Pictorial description of injectable hydrogels with desired features. (A) Covalent cross-linking drastically improves the stiffness of a hydrogel. (B) Elasticity can be improved through the use of supramolecular interactions and inorganic fillers. (C) Adhesiveness is enhanced using catechol groups or nanoparticles with proper dimensions and composition. anchors.text: Figure 1 | Cartilage regeneration techniques. a | A full-thickness focal chondral lesion. b | The lesion is debrided to ensure healthy, stable margins for integration of the host tissue with the neotissue. c | Microfracture. Channels are created using a 45° awl, spaced 3–4 mm apart, and 3–4 mm deep to penetrate the subchondral bone, allowing MSCs to migrate from the marrow to the cartilage defect. d | ACI. The debrided lesion is filled with 12–48 million autologous chondrocytes and covered with a periosteal flap or mixed collagen type I and type III membrane. e | MACI. The autologous chondrocyte population is expanded in vitro and then seeded for 3 days onto an absorbable 3D (collagen types I and III or hyaluronic acid) matrix prior to implantation. The cell-seeded scaffold is then secured into the lesion with fibrin glue. Abbreviations: ACI, autologous chondrocyte implantation; MACI, matrix-assisted autologous chondrocyte implantation; MSC, mesenchymal stem cell.

Figure 2 | Algorithm for treatment of cartilage defects. If rehabilitation is not a viable option for a patient with a symptomatic cartilage lesion, the surgeon should assess both the size and location of the defect, determine whether the patient desires a more active (high demand) or sedentary (low demand) lifestyle, and consider if the patient has undergone previous cartilage repair treatments. *Recommended treatment options for a given situation. $ ^{115} $

Figure 3 | New tissue engineering techniques for treating cartilage lesions. a | Technically mimicking ACI, a debrided chondral lesion is filled with bone-marrow-derived or chondroinduced MSCs, not autologous chondrocytes, and covered with a collagen type I/III membrane. b | Intra-articular injection of MSCs with or without injectable matrices is a single-stage procedure. c | AMIC is a cell-free, scaffold-based single surgery. Microfracture releases blood and bone marrow MSCs, then collagen type I/III, hyaluronic acid or fibrin matrix are sutured or glued into the defect. d | MACI uses scaffolds plus either primary articular chondrocytes or bone-marrow-derived MSCs. e | Neotissue can be formed by combining particulated native cartilage with fibrin glue. Limited autodigestion of ECM releases superficial chondrocytes, which then produce additional ECM that integrates the cartilage particles and fills the defect. f | Scaffold-free techniques include a self-assembling process or chondrospheres. Without a scaffold to interrupt cell-cell signalling and stress shielding, cells are able to respond to stimuli and promote integration of neotissue ECM with the surrounding tissue. Resulting neotissue is thought to be a bioactive microenvironment. Abbreviations: ACI, autologous chondrocyte implantation; AMIC, autologous matrix-induced chondrogenesis; ECM, extracellular matrix; MACI, matrix-induced autologous chondrocyte implantation; MSC, mesenchymal stem cell.

Figure 4 | The tissue engineering paradigm. Cells, signals and scaffolds are the major elements of tissue engineering approaches to cartilage repair. For this purpose, many different cell sources (autologous cells, allogeneic cells or stem cells) have been tested in vitro. Neotissue has been cultured ex vivo with various stimuli and chemicals to enhance synthesis and chondrogenic potential. To further improve the integrity of neotissues, scaffolds have been used to create a 3D environment to maintain the phenotype of cells, carry integrated cells in vivo, and to recruit cells from the host environment. Combinations of these factors drive the three major cartilage engineering strategies that exist: cell-free, scaffold-based implants that promote cell recruitment with chemoattractants; cell-seeded scaffolds that mimic the structure of native tissues; and scaffold-free, cell-based biomimetic techniques. Abbreviations: AMIC, autologous matrix-induced chondrogenesis; ECM, extracellular matrix; GAG, glycosaminoglycans; MACI, matrix-assisted autologous chondrocyte implantation.

anchors.text: FIGURE 1: Microstructure and pathological changes of normal and damaged cartilage. Articular cartilage is divided into surface layer, middle layer, deep layer, calcified layer, and subchondral bone [20]. Normal cartilage is rich in type II collagen and ECM. When cartilage is damaged, it is usually repaired into fibrocartilage, which is rich in type I collagen. The internal manifestations of the damaged cartilage are chondrocyte hypertrophy and vascular invasion.

FIGURE 2: Microenvironmental factors affecting cartilage regeneration. Articular cartilage regeneration is affected by many factors. Excessive mechanical stress stimulation, such as hydrostatic force, shear force, and compression force [50]. Some cytokines are produced by senescent cells, such as IL-6, IL-17, and TNF- $ \alpha $ [51]. The change of oxygen partial pressure resulted in the decrease of glutathione (GSH)/oxidized glutathione (GSSG) ratio and the increase of superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1) and superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2) protein expression [52]. The decrease of growth factors such as transforming growth factor- $ \beta $ (TGF- $ \beta $), insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), and platelet-rich plasma (PRP) [53]. All these factors inhibit the regeneration of cartilage.

FIGURE 3: TRPV4-mediated mechanotransduction. Under physiological dynamic load, the TRPV4 ion channel is activated,  $ Ca^{2+} $ influx promotes the expression of type II collagen (Col II) and aggrecan (ACAN) and reduces the expression of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) [64].

FIGURE 4: Therapeutic strategies for mechanical stimulation. GSK101 activates the TRPV4 channel, which in turn enhances the expression of type II collagen and aggrecan [74]. GsMTx4 inhibits the opening of Piezo1 channels, and Verapamil inhibits VGCC channels, which together regulate ca $ ^{2+} $ homeostasis under abnormal load, thereby protecting chondrocytes [64].

FIGURE 5: Piezo1-mediated mechanotransduction. Under the stimulation of excessive mechanical load and IL- $ 1\alpha $, ca $ ^{2+} $ enters the cells through the Piezo1 channel, increasing the expression of Piezo1 and MMPs and increasing the mechanical sensitivity of chondrocytes to mechanical loads [81].

FIGURE 6: The interaction between immune cells in microenvironment. When cartilage is damaged, neutrophils are first recruited to secrete pro-inflammatory mediators. Macrophages, DCs, and NK cells are subsequently recruited [124]. Th1 cells polarize M0 macrophages into M1 macrophages under the stimulation of IFN- $ \gamma $. DCs induce activation of Th1 and Th17, leading to cartilage degradation. Th2 cells secrete IL-4, which polarizes M0 macrophages into M2 macrophages, inhibits inflammation, and promotes cartilage repair [20].

anchors.text: Fig. 2 | Approaches for tissue engineering cartilage in an inflammatory environment. The presence of inflammation in affected joints in osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis affects joint physiology, and if inflammation is not reduced it is likely to affect cartilage-based joint treatments. Immunomodulatory approaches in combination with tissue engineering might be needed to treat these inflamed joints. a, Inflamed joints that are affected by osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis, various degenerative and pathological changes occur, and immune cells invade. b, Several immunomodulatory techniques have been used

Fig. 3 | The translational vector for tissue-engineered cartilage products.
The translational vector is the process from research and development to clinical use, and it requires the fulfilment of multiple steps in the domains of regulation, manufacturing, and funding and intellectual property (IP). a. The aspects of the translational vector must be coordinated in parallel as they influence each other simultaneously in an interconnected manner. For example, an investigator might only be able to secure the appropriate funding to conduct costly clinical trials after IP is established. b. In the USA, the multiple successive steps of regulatory approval required for development of biologics or devices for cartilage tissue engineering are managed by the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER) or the Center for Devices and Radiological Health (CDRH), respectively. c. Successive stages in the manufacture of tissue-engineered cartilage products (for use in animal studies, clinical trials and clinical-grade products) are each subject to specific manufacturing quality requirements. d. Translation of a product from research to clinical use requires escalating funding and appropriate management of IP. BLA, Biologics License Application; GLP, Good Laboratory Practice; GMP, Good Manufacturing Practice; IDE, Investigational Device Exemption; IND, Investigational New Drug; PMA, Premarket Approval.

to modulate the immune response within inflamed joints. Drug- and cell-based immunomodulatory injections, with or without a carrier, have been used to modulate inflammation but do not repair the underlying cartilage damage. As an alternative to injection-based approaches, tissue immunoengineering involves the deployment of a mechanically robust implant with immunomodulatory properties. Two categories of treatment developed within the field of tissue immunoengineering are the use of immunomodulatory biomaterials and synthetic biology.

anchors.text: Fig 1 | Upper panel: graphical illustration of bias-variance trade-off. The training set is used to develop a model; the testing set is used to test it. A simple, underfitting model leads to high prediction error in training and testing sets. By increasing model complexity, the training set error can be lowered to zero. However, the testing set error (which needs to be minimised) only reduces to a point and then increases as complexity increases. The ideal model complexity is one that minimises the testing set error. An overfitting model might appear to perform well in the training set but might still be worthless—ie, overfitting leads to optimism. Lower three panels: fictional example of three prediction models (lines) developed using a dataset (points). x, y: single continuous predictor and outcome, respectively. The underfitting model has large training error and will also have large testing errors; the overfitting model performs perfectly in the development set (ie, zero training error) but will perform poorly in new data (large testing error). The ideal model complexity will perform better than the other two in new data.

Fig 2 | Results from a model predicting the probability of a patient with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis experiencing a relapse in the next two years. Figures adapted from Chalkou et al. $ ^{119} $ Upper panel: calibration plot. Solid blue line shows calibration using a LOESS (locally estimated scatterplot smoothing line), and shaded area shows 95% confidence intervals. Dotted blue line corresponds to perfect calibration. Maximum predicted probability was around 60% for this example. The model is well calibrated for predicted probabilities lower than 35%. Lower panel: decision curve analysis comparing net benefit of three strategies deciding on whether to intensify treatment in patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (from no treatment to first line treatment, or from first line to second line treatment, etc). The strategies are to continue current treatment (do not intensify), to intensify treatment for all, or to intensify treatment according to predictions from model considering probability of experiencing a relapse in the next two years—i.e., if predicted probability is higher than a threshold (shown on x axis), then the treatment can be intensified.
Fig 3 | Graphical overview of 13 proposed steps for developing a clinical prediction model. TRIPOD=transparent reporting of a multivariable prediction model for individual prognosis or diagnosis

anchors.text: Fig. 1. Schematic of streaming potential mechanism in cartilage. The specimen is compressed by a porous electrode against an impermeable electrode in a cylindrically confined geometry. Upward fluid flow entrains mobile (+) counterions, leaving behind a small fraction of unneutralized negative molecular charge groups. This slight charge separation generates a streaming potential field which produces conduction currents that are antiparallel to the fluid flow. The measured open circuit potential represents the balance between convective charge separation and the tendency of the conduction currents to maintain electroneutrality, thereby ensuring zero net current.
Fig. 2. Schematic of test chamber for electromechanical transduction experiments with adult bovine articular cartilage specimens.

Fig. 3. Schematic of electrode configuration and circuit for measuring (a) the streaming potential (open-circuit voltage) generated by an applied displacement stimulus; (b) the streaming current (short-circuit current) using an op-amp in feedback configuration to maintain electrodes at the same potential; (c) the stress $\sigma$ generated by an applied current using a Kepco bipolar operational power supply driven by a Rockland Systems 5100 digital frequency synthesizer.

Fig. 4. (a) Dynamic load and streaming potential response for a specimen equilibrated in 0.05 M NaCl at neutral pH and tested with a static offset strain of 15% and a dynamic strain amplitude of 1%. Stress and streaming potential lead the displacement by the phase angles  $ \theta $ and  $ \psi $, respectively. Total harmonic distortion for this specimen reached approx. 5% for load and 5.5% for streaming potential by 1 Hz, mainly due to second harmonic.

Fig. 4. (a) Dynamic load and streaming potential response for a specimen equilibrated in 0.05 M NaCl at neutral pH and tested with a static offset strain of 15% and a dynamic strain amplitude of 1%. anchors.text: Figure 1. Review framework of piezoelectric biomaterials in osteochondral tissue engineering: from biological basis to translational prospects. The figure summarizes the overall logic of this review, beginning with the biological basis of biopiezoelectricity across hierarchical scales, followed by the structural and functional features of the osteochondral unit, the major regenerative bottlenecks in cartilage and osteochondral repair, the electromechanical regulatory mechanisms involved in tissue regeneration, representative material platforms for bone, cartilage, and osteochondral applications, and the key translational challenges and future directions.

Figure 2. Schematic illustration of mechanical-to-electrical signal conversion at the osteochondral interface and its biological consequences. Physiological joint loading, including compression, shear, and motion, induces extracellular matrix deformation and interstitial fluid movement within the osteochondral unit. These mechanical stimuli generate localized electrical cues through piezoelectric and electrokinetic mechanisms, including collagen-associated polarization, bound charge formation, and streaming potentials. The resulting electrical microenvironment is sensed by cells through ion channels such as VGCCs, Piezo channels, and TRPV4, leading to membrane depolarization,  $ Ca^{2+} $ influx, and activation of downstream signaling pathways. These events subsequently regulate chondrogenesis, osteogenesis, extracellular matrix synthesis, mineralization, and osteochondral interface integration.

anchors.text:
Fig. 1.
Differences in the physiologic environment and cellular make-up of bone and cartilage have profound effects on the potential to engineer these tissues. Through the presence of stem cells in marrow and in the periosteum, and access to abundant nutrients via vasculature, bone possesses inherent regenerative capability that can be harnessed in regenerative therapies. Cartilage's hypocellularity and lack of nutrient supply, coupled with the inability of bone marrow MSCs or resident chondroprogenitor cells to generate hyaline ECM, result in a tissue unable to mount a functional healing response. Thus, in contrast to bone's ability to heal, cartilage needs more robust exogenous approaches to achieve satisfactory regeneration.

Fig. 2.
Various clinical strategies regenerate cartilage using chondrocytes or MSCs. Microfracture involves subchondral bone penetration to release bone marrow that forms a stem cell-rich clot. Augmented microfracture adds a scaffold to the microfracture technique to concentrate and aid in stem cell differentiation. Acellular scaffolds are also used in full-thickness defects. Autologous chondrocyte implantation involves harvest of the patient's chondrocytes; the cells are expanded in vitro, and then placed under a collagen membrane sutured over the defect site. Advancement of this technique involves seeding chondrocytes onto a scaffold and culturing in vitro prior to implantation. Scaffoldless engineered cartilage formed in vitro with chondrocytes is also used with two products currently undergoing clinical trials. In aforementioned strategies, MSCs can be used instead of chondrocytes; however, products based on these technologies are at earlier stages of development. Osteochondral grafts taken either from less-load bearing regions of the patient's own joint or cadaveric joints are implanted to fill focal defects. Intra-articular injections (e.g., hyaluronan) reduce the symptoms of cartilage degeneration, but the effects are only temporary. Total joint replacement is the final option when cartilage damage is so extensive that no other therapies can be effective.

Fig. 3.

Scaffoldless tissue-engineering. The cell source chosen for cartilage generation, treated with appropriate culture conditions, must have the ability to produce matrix specific to articular cartilage and must not evoke an immune response. TGF- $ \beta $ family growth factors, physiologic mechanical stimulation, and matrix remodeling enzymes have shown a large degree of promise as stimuli.
